references.text: In [ref:Joh 5:10|John 5:10], the Jews accuse the healed man of carrying his bed on the Sabbath. The question in verse 12 follows directly from this accusation—they want to know who gave him that command.

In [ref:Joh 5:8-9|John 5:8-9], Jesus gives the command, "Take up your bed and walk!", which the Jewish leaders ask about in verse 12. They focus on the one who gave the order to carry the bed rather than on the healing itself.
[ref:Joh 5:13|John 5:13] explains why the man could not answer the question: he did not know who Jesus was, because Jesus had withdrawn from the crowd.

In [ref:Joh 9:15-16|John 9:15-16], the Pharisees interrogate the man born blind about how he was healed, in a similar way to how they ask here who commanded the man to carry his bed. Both cases show that the religious leaders were more concerned with Sabbath-breaking than with the miracle.

In [ref:Joh 9:24-26|John 9:24-26], the man born blind is repeatedly questioned by the Pharisees about who healed him. The pattern is the same as in John 5:12—focus on identifying the one who broke Sabbath rules.

In [ref:Joh 7:23|John 7:23], Jesus himself refers back to this healing and argues that if circumcision can be performed on the Sabbath, it should also be allowed to make a whole person well on the Sabbath.
[ref:2 Mos 20:10|Exodus 20:10] contains the Sabbath commandment forbidding work, which the Jewish leaders believed was broken. Their question in John 5:12 assumes this law.

[ref:Jer 17:21-22|Jeremiah 17:21-22] warns against carrying burdens on the Sabbath day. The Jewish leaders' question about who said "Take up and walk" reflects this tradition of forbidding the carrying of loads on the Sabbath.
